title: Cap. VIII open: adversaries' arguments proposed and solved
latin: Cap. VIII. Argumenta adversariorum proponuntur et solvuntur. Accedamus jam ad argumenta adversariorum, qui contendunt peccata ea cum quibus reprobi praevidentur vita decessuri, fuisse causam meritoriam et motivam reprobationis Divinae.
pass_a: Chapter VIII. The arguments of the adversaries are proposed and solved. Let us now approach the arguments of the adversaries, who contend that those sins with which the reprobate are foresighted as about to depart from life were the meritorious and moving cause of Divine reprobation.
pass_b: Chapter VIII — the adversaries' arguments proposed and solved. We turn now to their arguments: they contend that the sins with which the reprobate are foresighted as about to leave life were the meritorious and moving cause of divine reprobation.

lemmas.gloss: foresight sins as meritorious and moving cause

title: Cap. VIII: prefatory — not the will to damn, but the eternal denial of efficacious grace
latin: Sed priusquam horum rationes in medium afferantur, id praestruendum est: Non quaeri de reprobatione, quatenus denotat apud nonnullos Theologos voluntatem damnandi sive cruciandi reprobatos: Nam extra controversiam esse debet, hanc voluntatem Dei semper respicere peccatum ut meritoriam causam decretae punitionis. Sed quaeritur de reprobatione, quatenus denotat absolutum illud et aeternum Dei decretum, quo negavit ab aeterno Caino et Judae efficacem gratiam, quam illis praeparare et dare potuisset, si ita illi complacitum fuisset.
pass_a: But before the reasons of these are brought into the midst, this is to be prefaced: That it is not asked concerning reprobation, insofar as it denotes among some Theologians the will of damning or of tormenting the reprobated: For it ought to be outside controversy that this will of God always regards sin as the meritorious cause of the decreed punishment. But it is asked concerning reprobation, insofar as it denotes that absolute and eternal decree of God, by which from eternity he denied to Cain and Judas efficacious grace, which he could have prepared and given them, if it had so pleased him.
pass_b: Before their reasons are brought forward, this must be prefaced: we are not asking about reprobation as some theologians mean the will to damn or torment the reprobate — that will of God always regards sin as meritorious cause of decreed punishment, beyond dispute. We ask about reprobation as that absolute eternal decree by which from eternity God denied Cain and Judas efficacious grace he could have prepared and given them, had it so pleased him.

lemmas.gloss: not the will to damn (always regards sin)

title: Cap. VIII: those denied such grace are passed by — demerit concomitant, not cause of praeterition
latin: Quibus Deus in aeterno suo decreto talem gratiam eandemque ordinationem ad gloriam denegavit, eos non elegit sed praeteriit et, uti loquuntur Theologi, reprobavit. Illud etiam adjungendum est: Nos haud negare in omnibus hominibus, in quos cadit actus Divinae reprobationis, inveniri demeritum concomitans, vel subjecto adhaerescens: sed negamus praeteritionem illam sive non-electionem, quam reprobationem negativam vocamus, ex intuitu hujus demeriti profluxisse. Deus enim demeritum originale tam in electis quam reprobis intuetur, et tamen non pro discrimine causae, sed pro suo beneplacito vult eligere Jacobum, et non vult eligere, sed reprobare Esavum.
pass_a: Those to whom God in his eternal decree denied such grace and the same ordination unto glory, he did not elect but passed by and, as the Theologians speak, reprobated. This also is to be added: that we by no means deny that in all men upon whom the act of Divine reprobation falls, there is found a concomitant demerit, or adhering to the subject: but we deny that that passing by or non-election, which we call negative reprobation, flowed from the intuition of this demerit. For God regards original demerit both in the elect and in the reprobate, and yet not according to discrimination of cause, but according to his good pleasure he wills to elect Jacob, and wills not to elect, but to reprobate Esau.
pass_b: Those to whom God in his eternal decree denied such grace and the same ordination to glory, he did not elect but passed by — and, as theologians speak, reprobated. Add this: we do not deny that in all on whom divine reprobation falls there is found concomitant demerit adhering to the subject. What we deny is that that praeterition or non-election we call negative reprobation flowed from regard to that demerit. God sees original demerit in elect and reprobate alike — yet not by discrimination of cause, but by his good pleasure, he wills to elect Jacob, and wills not to elect but to reprobate Esau.

lemmas.gloss: same original demerit; difference by good pleasure

title: Cap. VIII: actual demerits foresight as consequent, not antecedent, to praeterition
latin: Quod autem attinet ad actualia demerita ex perseverantia finali in peccatis sive infidelitate orta, certum est et haec etiam praevideri ut futura in omnibus reprobis, sed ut futura concomitanter vel consequenter, non causaliter aut antecedenter ad actum praeteritionis Divinae. Non enim praeviderentur a Deo Cain aut Judas in improbitate sua et infidelitate morituri, nisi praesupposita antecedente Dei voluntate de non concedenda illis speciali gratia, qua emollirentur et ad fidem ac paenitentiam converterentur: quae negatio non-electionis sive reprobationis manifesta probatio est. Quis enim tam impie desipiat, ut dicat Deum malas hominum voluntates, quas voluerit quando voluerit, ubi voluerit, in bonum non posse convertere? ut recte Augustinus, Enchirid. cap. 98. Sed argumenta audiamus.
pass_a: But as to what pertains to actual demerits arisen from final perseverance in sins or unbelief, it is certain that these also are foresighted as future in all the reprobate, but as future concomitantly or consequently, not causally or antecedently to the act of Divine passing by. For Cain or Judas would not be foresighted by God as about to die in their wickedness and unbelief, unless the antecedent will of God concerning not granting them special grace, by which they would be softened and converted unto faith and penitence, were presupposed: which negation is a manifest proof of non-election or reprobation. For who would so impiously dote, as to say that God cannot convert the evil wills of men, which he has willed when he has willed, where he has willed, into good? as Augustine rightly, Enchiridion chapter 98. But let us hear the arguments.
pass_b: As for actual demerits from final perseverance in sins or unbelief: yes, these too are foresighted as future in all the reprobate — but as future concomitantly or consequently, not causally or antecedently to the divine act of praeterition. God would not foresee Cain or Judas dying in their wickedness and unbelief unless his prior will not to grant them special grace — by which they would be softened and turned to faith and penitence — were presupposed. That denial is plain proof of non-election or reprobation. Who would so impiously dote as to say God cannot turn evil human wills to good when, where, and as he wills? So Augustine rightly (Enchiridion 98). But let us hear the arguments.

lemmas.gloss: God can convert evil wills when he wills

title: Cap. VIII Arg. 1: Scripture — God does not will that men perish
latin: Reprobationem igitur fluere ex praevisis hominum demeritis, primo probare conantur nonnulli ex illis Scripturae locis, in quibus Deus dicitur nequaquam velle ut homines pereant: Quod minime verum esset, si Deus sola sua voluntate, et non propter peccata, tantam hominum multitudinem reprobaret. Huc afferunt illud Ezek. xviii. 23, Nunquid voluntatis meae est mors impii? et Hos. xiii. 9. Perditio tua ex te. Item illud Apostoli, 1 Tim. ii. 4. Deus vult omnes salvos fieri. Et illud Servatoris, Matth. xi. 28. Venite ad me omnes; ejusque generis loca alia quamplurima, quae sigillatim repetere aut discutere non est necesse.
pass_a: That reprobation therefore flows from the foresighted demerits of men, some first try to prove from those places of Scripture in which God is said by no means to will that men perish: Which would be least true, if God by his will alone, and not on account of sins, reprobated so great a multitude of men. Hither they bring that of Ezek. 18:23, Is the death of the wicked of my will? and Hos. 13:9. Thy destruction is from thee. Likewise that of the Apostle, 1 Tim. 2:4. God wills all to be made safe. And that of the Savior, Matt. 11:28. Come unto me all; and very many other places of that kind, which it is not necessary to repeat or discuss one by one.
pass_b: First they try to prove reprobation flows from foresighted human demerits from those Scripture places where God is said not to will that men perish — which would hardly be true, they say, if God by his will alone, and not for sins, reprobated so great a multitude. They cite Ezek. 18:23 (Is the death of the wicked of my will?), Hos. 13:9 (Your destruction is from you), 1 Tim. 2:4 (God wills all to be saved), Matt. 11:28 (Come to me, all), and many like places — no need to repeat or discuss them one by one.

lemmas.gloss: God does not will the death of the wicked
wills all saved; come unto me all

title: Cap. VIII Arg. 1 Resp.: simple complacence vs predestinating will; non-election is not willing to destroy
latin: Si id volunt adversarii, Deum seposita praevisione et consideratione antecedente demeritorum humanorum, velle ex aequo salutem universis hominibus, hoc nos negamus ex locis allegatis effici posse. Efficitur quidem, Deum voluntate simplicis complacentiae velle ut omnes credant, ut omnes resipiscant, ut nemo pereat, ut nemo damnetur; sed non efficitur, Deum voluntate praedestinante velle ex aequo, ante praevisionem demeritorum, in omnibus operari ut credant, ut resipiscant; operari ne pereant, ne damnentur: neque efficitur, Deum voluntate reprobante haud decrevisse negare quibusdam gratiam efficacem, et infallibilem ordinationem ad gloriam. Possunt enim haec duo simul consistere: Deus vult ut omnes credant, et nemo pereat, scilicet voluntate simplicis complacentiae; et, Deus vult permittere ut quidam in infidelitate sua voluntaria persistent, et ab aeterna salute deficiant. In eo igitur errant adversarii, quod sumunt haec duo, non-eligere sive reprobare, et velle perdere vel mortem aeternam inferre, pro aequipollentibus: cum non-electio vel praeteritio competere possit in creaturam integram, quod in angelis manifestum est; at voluntas perdendi vel morte aeterna afficiendi non potest cadere nisi in creaturam vitiatam: cum non-electio sit mera negatio gratuiti beneficii, Mors sive perditio sit stipendium commissi peccati. Est quidem verissimum, omnes non-electos infallibiliter ruituros in mortem aeternam: est etiam perspicuum, omnes non-electos ab aeterno positiva Dei voluntate huic morti adjudicatos: sed haec ad mortem deputatio non concipienda est ut in eodem signo rationis peracta, quo non-electio statuitur, sed in alio posteriore, quo non-electi perseverantia finalis in statu peccati praevidetur. Ex eo igitur quod Deus neminem vult perire absque antecedanea consideratione demeritorum, non sequitur, Deum neminem velle praeterire aut non-eligere absque antecedanea consideratione eorundem.
pass_a: If the adversaries mean this, that God, foresight and antecedent consideration of human demerits being set aside, wills salvation equally to all men, this we deny can be effected from the places alleged. It is indeed effected that God by the will of simple complacence wills that all believe, that all repent, that no one perish, that no one be damned; but it is not effected that God by predestinating will wills equally, before foresight of demerits, to work in all that they believe, that they repent; to work that they not perish, that they not be damned: nor is it effected that God by reprobating will has not decreed to deny to certain ones efficacious grace, and infallible ordination unto glory. For these two can stand together: God wills that all believe, and no one perish, namely by the will of simple complacence; and, God wills to permit that certain ones persist in their voluntary unbelief, and fall short of eternal salvation. In this therefore the adversaries err, that they take these two, not to elect or to reprobate, and to will to destroy or to inflict eternal death, as equipollent: whereas non-election or passing by can compete unto an intact creature, which is manifest in the angels; but the will of destroying or of affecting with eternal death cannot fall except upon a vitiated creature: since non-election is the mere negation of a gratuitous benefit, Death or perdition is the wage of committed sin. It is indeed most true that all the non-elect will infallibly rush into eternal death: it is also clear that all the non-elect from eternity by the positive will of God are adjudged to this death: but this deputing unto death is not to be conceived as performed in the same sign of reason in which non-election is established, but in another later, in which the final perseverance of the non-elect in the state of sin is foresighted. From this therefore that God wills no one to perish without antecedent consideration of demerits, it does not follow that God wills no one to pass by or not-elect without antecedent consideration of the same.
pass_b: If adversaries mean that God, foresight of human demerits set aside, wills salvation equally to all, we deny the cited places prove that. They do prove that by the will of simple complacence God wills that all believe and repent, that none perish or be damned. They do not prove that by predestinating will he wills equally, before foresight of demerits, to work in all so they believe and repent, and not perish or be damned — nor that by reprobating will he has not decreed to deny some efficacious grace and infallible ordination to glory. Those two can stand together: God wills that all believe and none perish (simple complacence); and God wills to permit some to persist in voluntary unbelief and fall short of eternal salvation. Adversaries err in taking not-to-elect (or to reprobate) as equipollent with willing to destroy or inflict eternal death. Non-election or praeterition can fall on an intact creature — plain in the angels — but the will to destroy or afflict with eternal death can fall only on a vitiated creature: non-election is mere denial of a gratuitous benefit; death or perdition is sin's wage. True: all the non-elect will infallibly rush into eternal death, and from eternity God's positive will adjudges them to it — but that deputing to death is not conceived in the same sign of reason as non-election, but in a later one where final perseverance in sin is foresighted. That God wills none to perish without prior regard to demerits does not entail that he wills none to pass by or not-elect without that same prior regard.

lemmas.gloss: will of simple complacence vs predestinating will
